intro: Five natural monuments, spread across three of Cologne's green spaces rather than the cathedral everyone photographs. The Flora botanical garden holds a wingnut with fourteen trunks from one base. A hospital park in Lindenthal, older than the hospital by a century, keeps the city's thickest measured trunk, a plane 5.30 metres round, and an oak nearby. The Volksgarten's Turkey oak was likely one of four hundred mature trees moved in to make the park look old on opening day, 1889. None of the five has a documented age yet, an honest gap this page asks readers to help close.
meta_description: Cologne's five natural monuments: a fourteen-trunked wingnut, the city's thickest measured tree, and a Turkey oak from the Volksgarten's 1889 opening.
question_meta: Cologne's oldest tree isn't dated yet: no age has been measured for any of its five natural monuments. Where they stand, and what would settle it.
question_answer: Nobody has measured the age of any of Cologne's five registered trees on this page, so there is no confirmed oldest yet. The strongest circumstantial case belongs to the Great Plane of Hohenlind, a London plane 5.30 metres round standing in a former country estate that was already reckoned about 150 years old in 1932, putting some of the estate's planting back into the late 1700s. That figure describes the park the tree grows in, not a dated record for the plane itself, so treat it as context rather than an age. If you know how to date any of these trees, or can supply a girth for the ones still unmeasured, tell us: this is exactly the kind of gap the site is built to close with readers rather than guesses.
question_context: Germany designates individual trees as Naturdenkmal, natural monuments, under state nature-conservation law, and Cologne keeps a public list of its own, reproduced in full on German Wikipedia as Liste der Naturdenkmale in Koln. It runs to roughly two hundred entries, mostly ordinary protected street trees, and none of them carry an age field: the register records girth, species and location, never when a tree was planted. Two of the five trees here were measured by the city in May 2018, at 5.30 and 3.75 metres round; the other three have no girth on file either, an honest gap rather than an oversight. What the register does supply reliably is provenance: three of these trees stand inside larger green spaces, the Flora botanical garden, the Volksgarten and the Stadtwald, each with its own documented history that explains why an old tree might be there, without dating the individual specimen itself. Ages across this page are left blank rather than guessed, and each is a real question a reader with a tape measure or a local record could help answer.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Cologne?
faq.a: Unconfirmed. None of the city's five registered natural monuments on this page has a documented age. The best circumstantial case is the Great Plane of Hohenlind, in a park estate already reckoned about 150 years old in 1932, though that dates the park rather than the tree itself.

faq.q: Are Cologne's trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes, all five. The Flora, the Volksgarten and the Koelner Stadtwald are public parks open at all hours or until dusk. The Hohenlind trees stand in a hospital's grounds, but the green space itself, not the hospital building, is stated by the hospital and independent sources to be open to the public in daytime.

faq.q: Why does a hospital park hold two of Cologne's natural monuments?
faq.a: St. Elisabeth-Krankenhaus Koln-Hohenlind was built in 1927 into an existing country estate park that already had its own mature planting, some of it reckoned around 150 years old by 1932. The hospital inherited the park rather than planting it.

faq.q: What species is the fourteen-trunked tree at the Flora?
faq.a: A Caucasian wingnut (Pterocarya fraxinifolia), registered as a single natural monument with fourteen daughter trunks growing from one base. A second, ordinary single-trunked wingnut is registered nearby in the same garden, so look for the multiple trunks to tell them apart.

trees.name: The Fourteen-Trunked Caucasian Wingnut

location.address: Botanischer Garten / Flora, Amsterdamer Strasse 34, 50735 Koln

verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkmale_in_K%C3%B6ln (register entry ND 503.03/20: 'Kaukasische Fluegelnuss mit 14 Tochterstaemmen, Flora / Botanischer Garten am Weg zum Gebaeude des Landesverb. Gartenbau Rheinland')

https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flora_(K%C3%B6ln) (garden history: opened 1864-08-14 on the site vacated when the old botanical garden near the cathedral made way for the main station; Caucasian wingnuts and Ginkgos are named among species planted at the garden's founding, though not tied by name to this specific specimen)
trees.access: Free, no ticket. The garden (Flora / Botanischer Garten) is open daily 8am until dusk, at most until 9pm.
trees.transport: Koln-Riehl, tram lines 16 and 18 to 'Zoo/Flora' stop, then a short walk into the garden.
trees.story:
The Great Wingnut of the Flora sends up fourteen trunks from a single base, which is not how Caucasian wingnuts usually grow. Most stay to one, or split into a modest two or three; this one has been suckering and re-rooting into a thicket for long enough that Cologne's own natural-monument register lists it as a single designated tree with fourteen daughter stems.

It stands in the Flora, the city's botanical garden in Riehl, opened in 1864 on the ground the old botanical garden gave up when the main railway station needed the space nearer the cathedral. Wingnuts and ginkgos were among the species planted when the garden was new, which puts this tree's species on site since the founding, though nothing on record says this exact multi-trunked specimen is that old rather than a later addition. A second, single-trunked Caucasian wingnut is registered nearby, so look for the fourteen trunks rather than the species alone.

No girth or age has been recorded against it, an honest gap rather than an oversight: a tape measure around any one of the fourteen trunks would be a start. The garden is free and open daily until dusk, tram to Zoo/Flora and a short walk in.

best_time.label: July to September: long green catkins of winged nutlets hang from every branch

trees.name: The Great Plane of Hohenlind Park

location.address: Park of St. Elisabeth-Krankenhaus Koln-Hohenlind, Werthmannstrasse 1-3, 50935 Koln

verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkmale_in_K%C3%B6ln (register entry NDI 303.11c: Platanus x acerifolia, park of St. Elisabeth-Krankenhaus Koln-Hohenlind, trunk girth 5.30 m measured 2018-05-11, tree-level coordinates and OSM node given)

https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Elisabeth-Krankenhaus_K%C3%B6ln-Hohenlind (confirms the park predates the hospital, describes it as already an old estate park by the time a classicist country house stood here around 1850 and already about 150 years old by 1932; states plainly 'Die Gruenanlage ist tagsueber fuer die Oeffentlichkeit geoeffnet', the green space is open to the public during daytime hours)
trees.access: Free, open to the public during daytime hours. This is the hospital's surrounding park, not the hospital building itself; the grounds are open, the building is not part of the visit.
trees.transport: Koln-Lindenthal. Bus stop 'Werthmannstrasse' on Duererner Strasse (KVB line 136), then a short walk into the park.
trees.story:
The biggest-girthed tree found in this pass of Cologne stands in a hospital car park, more or less. St. Elisabeth-Krankenhaus Koln-Hohenlind was built in 1927 into a park that already existed, and the park is older than anyone at the hospital: a country estate stood here with its own grounds from around 1850, and a 1932 account already called the planting roughly 150 years old by then, putting parts of it back into the late eighteenth century.

The plane that survived all of it measures 5.30 metres round, measured by the city in 2018 and easily the thickest trunk this pass turned up anywhere in Cologne. It shares the grounds with a second, smaller plane and a pedunculate oak about a hundred metres away, all three separately designated natural monuments on the same old estate.

What looks like private hospital land is not: both the hospital's own materials and independent sources state plainly that the green space stays open to the public during the day, the grounds rather than the building. No age is recorded for the tree itself, only for the park around it, so treat the girth as the honest measure and the century estimate as a description of the ground it grows on, not a birth certificate.

trees.name: The Hohenlind Oak

location.address: Park of St. Elisabeth-Krankenhaus Koln-Hohenlind, Werthmannstrasse 1-3, 50935 Koln

verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkmale_in_K%C3%B6ln (register entry NDI 303.11b: Quercus robur, park of St. Elisabeth-Krankenhaus Koln-Hohenlind, trunk girth 3.75 m measured 2018-05-11, tree-level coordinates and OSM node given)

https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Elisabeth-Krankenhaus_K%C3%B6ln-Hohenlind (same park history and public-access statement as kol_002; names this oak specifically, 'eine Stieleiche (Quercus robur, NDI 303.11b)', among the park's protected trees)
trees.access: Free, open to the public during daytime hours. Part of the same estate park as kol_002, roughly 100 m away on foot.
trees.transport: Koln-Lindenthal. Bus stop 'Werthmannstrasse' on Duererner Strasse (KVB line 136), then a short walk into the park.
trees.story:
A hundred metres from the big plane in the Hohenlind hospital park stands a pedunculate oak, 3.75 metres round, on the same patch of former estate ground that predates the hospital by the better part of a century.

The two trees make one short walk rather than two separate trips, both listed as natural monuments in Cologne's own designation register and both measured by the city on the same day in May 2018. The oak has no recorded age of its own, but the estate around it was already reckoned about 150 years old in a 1932 account, which puts at least some of its planting into the late 1700s, a fact about the park rather than a dated certificate for this particular trunk.

A third registered tree, a second plane, stands nearby too, though without a published girth or coordinate to go with it, which is why it stays a lead rather than a fourth stop on this walk.

The park belongs to St. Elisabeth-Krankenhaus, a hospital, and both the hospital and independent sources confirm the grounds stay open to the public in daytime hours. The building is not part of the visit; the trees around it are.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Turkey Oak of the Volksgarten

location.address: Volksgarten, near the lakeside restaurant, Volksgartenstrasse, 50677 Koln

verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkmale_in_K%C3%B6ln (register entry ND 102.01b: Zerreiche/Quercus cerris, 'Volksgarten nordwestlich des Restaurants am Teich', northwest of the lakeside restaurant)

https://www.eghn.org/en/koelner-volksgarten-a-garden-monument-with-a-long-history/ (European Garden Heritage Network history of the park: opened 1889 under designer Adolf Kowallek; names Turkey oak explicitly among the exotic species 'planted on exposed locations in the meadows and near the water shore', and records that roughly 400 older trees transplanted from other woodland gave the new park a mature character from the start)
trees.access: Free, public park, no ticket. One of Cologne's main city parks.
trees.transport: Koln-Neustadt-Sued/Suedstadt. KVB tram/U-Bahn lines serving Chlodwigplatz or Ubierring, then a walk into the park; the tree stands near the lakeside restaurant by the park's pond.
trees.story:
Cologne's Volksgarten opened in 1889 with a shortcut nobody does anymore: its designer transplanted roughly four hundred already-mature trees in from other woodland so the new park would look established from its first season rather than take fifty years to grow into itself.

The Turkey oak by the lakeside restaurant was very likely one of the exotic accents chosen for that opening planting, set deliberately near the water where visitors would pass it. Turkey oak is an uncommon choice for a Rhineland park, native further south and east, which is presumably why it was picked to stand out rather than blend in. No source ties this individual tree to the 1889 planting by name, so treat the connection as circumstantial rather than dated fact, and no girth or age has been measured against it in the city's own register.

It keeps company nearby with a small group of Japanese pagoda trees at the park entrance and a swamp cypress at the pond's far edge, both worth finding on the same visit even though neither has cleared this pass's evidence bar yet.

The Volksgarten is one of Cologne's main city parks, free and open, reachable from Chlodwigplatz or Ubierring.

trees.name: The Moltke Lime of the Kahnweiher

location.address: Koelner Stadtwald, near the Kahnweiher (rowing pond), Mommsenstrasse/Duerener Strasse, 50931 Koln

verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkmale_in_K%C3%B6ln (register entry ND 303.01c: Tilia moltkei, 'Mommsenstrasse/Duerener Strasse, Stadtwald, Kahnweiher'; two blood beeches, ND 303.01a and 303.01b, are registered at the same spot)

https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6lner_Stadtwald (independent confirmation of the Kahnweiher pond's existence and coordinates inside the Stadtwald, a public recreation park built out from 1895/96; the article notes the park incorporates 'alte Baumbestaende' (old tree stocks) from earlier estates on the site, though it does not name this specific lime and says most of today's Stadtwald trees are under 80 years old, this individual being an exception as a registered natural monument)
trees.access: Free, public city forest/park (Koelner Stadtwald), no ticket, open at all times as public green space.
trees.transport: Koln-Lindenthal/Sued. Bus or tram to the Stadtwald/Aachener Strasse area, then a walk to the Kahnweiher (rowing-boat pond); roughly 1.5 km from the Hohenlind park trees (kol_002/kol_003).
trees.story:
Most of the Koelner Stadtwald is younger than it looks. The park was laid out from 1895 onward as a purpose-built recreation ground, and its own history notes that most of what grows there today is under eighty years old, ordinary planting for a public forest of that age.

The Moltke lime by the Kahnweiher, the park's rowing pond, is one of the exceptions: a comparatively uncommon large-leaved lime hybrid old enough to have earned individual protection as a city natural monument, standing where the Stadtwald's own account says older tree stock was folded in from estates that predated the park itself. Nothing on record gives this specific tree a planting date, so its age stays an honest gap rather than a guess, and the case for its age rests on inference about the ground rather than a measurement of the trunk.

Two registered copper beeches grow at the same spot, close enough to make this corner of the Stadtwald a small three-tree cluster rather than a single stop. Existence here rests on the city's own designation register alone. Nothing contradicts it, and the register has been reliable everywhere else in this city, but it is the thinnest-evidenced of Cologne's trees so far.

The Stadtwald is public land, free and open at all times, a walk of about 1.5 kilometres from the Hohenlind trees.
